text: A load-balanced web tier needs two more pieces of Azure plumbing on top of the VNet and NSG you already built: a public IP for the outside world to actually reach, and a load balancer to spread incoming traffic across whatever VMs are sitting behind it. This lesson covers the real Azure SKUs and mechanics, building directly on the generic load-balancing concept the earlier networking fundamentals course already taught in the abstract.

Azure Public IPs come in two SKUs, and only one matters anymore. Basic SKU was retired for new deployments by September 30, 2025 — no zone support, no SLA, and open by default, relying entirely on NSGs to restrict access. Standard SKU is zone-redundant, carries a 99.99% SLA across zones, and is secure by default: every inbound packet is denied unless an NSG explicitly allows it. Standard always uses static allocation, so the address never changes once assigned.

Azure Load Balancer is Azure's specific implementation of that load-balancing concept, and it operates at Layer 4 — distributing TCP and UDP traffic purely by IP address and port, never looking inside the actual application payload. That's deliberately different from Application Gateway, a Layer 7 service that does inspect content, which is outside this lesson's scope.

Three pieces have to be wired together for it to actually work: a backend pool holding the VMs that receive traffic, a health probe that periodically checks each one, and a rule mapping a frontend IP and port to that backend pool. Any instance that fails enough consecutive probes gets pulled out of rotation automatically until it passes again.

Because Standard SKU is secure by default, skipping the NSG allow rule is the single most common reason a perfectly configured load balancer still shows zero healthy backends — both the client traffic and the health probe's own traffic get silently dropped, even though every setting on the load balancer itself is correct. Next: connecting two separate VNets together so their resources can actually reach each other over Azure's own backbone.
